title: Avianca 052
summary: Avianca Flight 052 ran out of fuel after three holding patterns and a failed landing attempt at JFK, crashing onto a hillside in Cove Neck on Long Island. Due to poor communication and inadequate fuel management, the flight became critically low on fuel but controllers did not recognize the emergency because pilots failed to use the word 'emergency'. The crew's failure to properly declare a fuel emergency and inadequate traffic flow management by the FAA contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: The flight crew failed to properly declare a fuel emergency and inadequately managed the fuel load. Poor communication between crew and controllers and lack of standardized terminology for emergency fuel states contributed.

factors.evidence: The Boeing 707 flying this route ran out of fuel after a failed attempt to land at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).
First Officer Klotz radioed the controller, saying, 'ah well I think we need priority we're passing [unintelligible]'.
This dire situation was not recognized as an emergency by the controllers because of the failure of the pilots to use the word 'emergency'.
The flight was placed in three holding patterns.
The Boeing 707 flying this route crashed on a hillside in the small village of Cove Neck, New York.

events.text: Flight 052 entered its first holding pattern over Norfolk at 19:04.
The flight was placed in a second holding pattern from 19:43 to 20:12.
The flight entered its third holding pattern from 20:18 to 20:47.
At 21:24:06, the captain asked the first officer to tell them we are in an emergency.
The aircraft crashed on a hillside in the small village of Cove Neck, New York.

title: Indian Airlines 605
summary: Indian Airlines Flight 605, an Airbus A320, crashed onto a golf course near Bangalore Airport on February 14, 1990 while attempting to land. The crew selected the 'Open descent' automation mode rather than 'Glideslope capture', causing the aircraft to descend well below the correct flight path. Despite radio altitude call-outs warning of the descent, the crew failed to advance throttles or correct the trajectory in time.
probable_cause: The crew selected the incorrect flight control mode ('Open descent/flight idle' rather than 'Glideslope capture'), which allowed the aircraft to sink far below the correct approach path. The crew were unaware of their dangerously low position and reacted too late to the altitude call-outs.

factors.evidence: the pilots selecting the 'Open descent/flight idle' control mode rather than 'Glideslope capture'
the crew of Flight 605 weren't aware of the situation and the danger they were facing at the time
they further failed to advance the throttles or pull up even after the radio altitude call-outs
crashed onto a golf course while attempting to land at Bangalore

events.text: Bangalore Radar cleared Flight 605 to turn right and make visual approach to Runway 09
Crew disengaged autopilot and switched to Bangalore Tower frequency
Crew selected Open descent mode rather than Glideslope capture, allowing descent below glide path
Radio altitude call-outs warning of descent received by crew
Landing gear touched down on golf course approximately 2800 feet from airport

notes: Crew were under-trained on A320 systems
Similar accident occurred less than 2 years later
Captain Fernandez was undergoing qualification route check

title: 1990 Guangzhou Baiyun airport collisions
summary: On 2 October 1990, a hijacked Boeing 737-200 operating Xiamen Airlines Flight 8301 collided with two other aircraft at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport while attempting to land. The hijacked aircraft struck parked China Southwest Airlines Flight 4305, a Boeing 707, first, then collided with CAAC Flight 3523, a Boeing 757 waiting to take off, flipping onto its back. A total of 128 people were killed, including seven of nine crew members and 75 of 93 passengers on Flight 8301 and 46 of 110 passengers on Flight 3523, making the incident the deadliest aircraft hijacking prior to the September 11 attacks.
probable_cause: The hijacking led to collision with parked aircraft. The hijacker demanded diversion to Taiwan, but the aircraft was directed to land at Baiyun Airport instead. Procedural failures in handling the hijacking were acknowledged by authorities.

factors.evidence: Jiang Xiaofeng displayed wires in his hand and claimed he was carrying 7 kilograms of explosives, demanding that the flight be diverted to Taiwan.
Authorities acknowledged procedural failures in handling the hijacking.
The hijacked aircraft collided with two other aircraft at the old Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport.
The hijacked aircraft struck parked China Southwest Airlines Flight 4305 first, a Boeing 707, then collided with CAAC Flight 3523, a Boeing 757 waiting to take off, flipping onto its back.

events.text: Jiang Xiaofeng left his seat, rushed toward the cockpit holding a black plastic box, forcefully pounded on the cockpit door and opened it, displaying wires and claiming to carry explosives.
Jiang ordered that everyone except the captain leave the cockpit, and cockpit audio was transmitted to the control tower via radio communication systems.
The Civil Aviation Administration's Central South Regional Bureau authorized the aircraft to land at any airport, and Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport was shut down.
The hijacked aircraft struck parked China Southwest Airlines Flight 4305 first, then collided with CAAC Flight 3523, a Boeing 757 waiting to take off.

title: Alitalia 404
summary: Alitalia Flight 404, a DC-9, was on approach to Zurich Airport when the captain's instrument landing system display malfunctioned due to a faulty NAV receiver, incorrectly indicating the aircraft was 1,000 feet higher than its actual altitude. The first officer's ILS display was working correctly and showed the dangerously low approach. Without thoroughly examining which value was correct, the captain decided to ignore the first officer and aborted the first officer's go-around attempt. The aircraft subsequently struck Stadlerberg Mountain at 1,660 feet, killing all 46 occupants. The faulty receiver also prevented the autopilot and ground proximity warning system from receiving proper signals.
probable_cause: A short circuit in the captain's NAV receiver caused it to display incorrect altitude information while preventing the autopilot and GPWS from functioning. The captain's failure to respond to the first officer's warnings and attempt to override the go-around initiated by the first officer, combined with inadequate crew resource management, resulted in controlled flight into terrain.

factors.evidence: A short circuit in the captain's VOR/ILS receiver caused navigation instruments to indicate zero deviation with no failure warning flag.
The faulty receiver prevented the autopilot and ground proximity warning system from receiving proper course and glide path deviation signals.
The captain vetoed the first officer's attempted go-around without thoroughly examining which instrument reading was correct.
The aircraft descended to 1,660 feet and struck terrain while the crew believed they were on the correct glide path.
The absence of a failure warning flag on the malfunctioning receiver allowed the crew to rely on incorrect data.
The ground proximity warning system did not sound an alarm because the faulty receiver prevented it from receiving proper glide path information.
The aircraft struck Stadlerberg Mountain at 1,660 feet, killing all 40 passengers and 6 crew members.

events.text: The captain's ILS display gave incorrect values due to a faulty receiver, falsely indicating the aircraft was about 1,000 feet higher than its actual position.
The first officer's ILS display worked correctly and displayed the dangerously low approach, indicating the aircraft was much lower than the captain's display showed.
Without thoroughly examining which value was correct, the captain decided to ignore the first officer's display and aborted the go-around initiated by the first officer.
The aircraft continued descent with both autopilot and GPWS unable to warn because the faulty receiver prevented proper signal reception.

The aircraft struck Stadlerberg Mountain at 1,660 feet, with initial impact on trees on the right side followed by asymmetric lift and roll to the right before final impact in nearly inverted position.

notes: Faulty NAV receiver was primary technical cause
CRM breakdown (captain override of first officer) critical contributing factor

title: Bangkok Airways 125
summary: The Dash 8 was on approach to Samui Airport in bad weather when the crew decided to go around after losing sight of the runway. With little visual reference in low visibility, the crew became spatially disoriented. Confusion in communication between ATC and pilots about turn direction led to aggressive control inputs. The aircraft stalled in a steep left bank and crashed into trees.
probable_cause: Pilot spatial disorientation caused by conducting approach in minimal visual reference, combined with poor crew coordination, channelized attention focused on finding the runway, and aggressive control inputs that caused an aerodynamic stall.

factors.evidence: Bad weather, little to no visual reference at Samui Airport
Pilots suffered spatial disorientation amidst left turn in minimal visibility
Confusion in communication between ATC and pilots over direction to turn, poor cockpit coordination
Crew made abrupt and severe control inputs, full left wheel movement and left rudder input exacerbating roll to 89 degrees
Crew became entirely fixated on looking outside to spot runway, failed to monitor flight instruments
Aircraft stalled after reaching 89 degrees bank angle and 36 degrees nose-down attitude
Aircraft crashed into coconut and mango grove in 75-degree left bank and 36-degree nose-down attitude

events.text: Aircraft on approach to Samui Airport in bad weather with low visibility
Pilots decided to go around after losing sight of runway, declared they could not see runway
Tower controller advised crew: 'There is a hill on the right hand side, make a left turn out'
Crew applied full left wheel movement and left rudder while aircraft already in left bank, rolling to 89 degrees
Aircraft stalled and dived into coconut and mango grove 5 km southwest of airport in 75-degree left bank and 36-degree nose-down attitude
